All money is in $M and all values are illustrative.
This page records what the analysis assumes, how much the answer moves when those assumptions change, and the checks that the numbers are computed correctly. It is the place to start before using any figure from this site in a real decision.

title: Governance
text:
Limitations

Synthetic firm. Every cost and probability is illustrative; a real decision needs the firm’s own outage cost, restore-test results and leak exposure.
Posted demand. The crew names one price. Negotiated discounts exist, so treating the demand as final overstates the cost of paying.
No cyber insurance. Insurance would cover part of the outage and possibly the ransom, which shifts the walk-away point.
One crew. The model has a single crew that learns from our history. Several crews, or crews that share intelligence, would change how fast reputation builds.
Leak cost is fixed. It does not depend on the number or sensitivity of the records taken.
The targeting response is uncertain. The reputation result holds only if crews favor known payers: above about 0.24 for our firm and 0.59 for the fragile firm; see the Decision Map & Reputation page.
The crew learns about our walk-away point, not our policy. A firm that never pays looks like one with a low walk-away point, so its demand keeps falling instead of the crew moving on.
The staged path needs time. Restoring first and paying only if backups fail assumes the firm can negotiate while restoring; leak deadlines or rising demands can remove that option.
Sanctions are a cost, not a bar. A known sanctions link would rule out payment entirely rather than add a penalty.
Outage cost is constant per day. In practice client churn accelerates after the first week, which would make restore time matter even more.
The decryptor works fully or not at all. Partial decryption would leave some restore effort even after paying.

The result column shows whether it passed, and the detail column gives the evidence: the size of any error, the number of cases checked, or the values compared. A failure stops the build, so a published page should never show one.

text: All money is in $M and all values are illustrative. The firm is synthetic.

title: The Game
text:
The setup
A ransomware crew has encrypted the production platform of a 500-person fintech software firm and copied its client data. The crew posts a single demand. The firm can pay the demand, refuse and restore from backups, or combine the two: start restoring at once and pay only if the backups fail. The firm is a privately held company licensed by New York’s Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), and several of its clients are listed companies.
Each side knows different things. The firm knows its own restore time and how much it trusts its backups. The crew doesn’t; it can only guess from what it has seen of firms like ours. The crew wants the largest payment it can get, and the firm wants the cheaper path.
The data theft is treated separately from the encryption, because paying does not reliably buy silence. Coveware puts it bluntly: “threat actors’ promises to delete stolen data cannot be verified” (Coveware, October 2026). Whichever path we choose, some chance of a public leak remains.

title: The Game
text:
Three paths


Display code
comp_order <- c("Outage", "Data leak", "Ransom", "Sanctions exposure", "Payment costs")
tp <- wa$two_paths |>
  mutate(
    component = factor(COMPONENT_LABELS[component], levels = rev(comp_order)),
    path = factor(path, levels = rev(unique(path)))
  )
totals <- tp |> summarise(total = sum(cost), .by = path)
ggplot(tp, aes(cost, path, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = if_else(cost >= 0.9, fmt_num(cost, 1), "")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.8, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(data = totals, aes(total, path, label = fmt_m(total, 2)), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            hjust = -0.15, size = 4.2, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = COMPONENT_COLS, breaks = comp_order, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous("Expected cost ($M)", limits = c(0, 12.5), breaks = seq(0, 10, 2.5), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(22)) +
  labs(y = NULL,
       title = "Restoring first and paying only if backups fail is cheapest",
       subtitle = "Expected cost of each path at base inputs ($M)")








Figure 1: Expected cost of three paths at base inputs and a $2.5M demand. The staged path assumes a failed restore is discovered after 2 days.






How to read the plot. Each bar is one path, built from the costs we expect along it. The colored segments show where the money goes: lost operations while systems are down, a possible public leak of client data and, where a payment is made, the ransom, the sanctions penalty risk and the legal and filing costs of paying. The bottom bar starts restoring at once and pays only if the backups turn out to have failed, so its payment costs are small.
What the plot tells you. Restoring costs $10.70M and paying on day one $10.83M, about 1% apart, well inside the model’s uncertainty. Restoring first and paying only if backups fail costs $9.23M, less than either. Paying on day one shortens the outage but does not end it: the decryptor sometimes fails, and decryption itself takes days. The staged path wins because the ransom is paid only in the minority of incidents where backups fail.

The staged path wins because it turns a payment into a fallback for backup failure. With backup credibility of 0.80, a payment comes into question in only 20% of incidents, so backup credibility decides whether a payment is ever needed. The path stays cheapest even if a failed restore takes 7 days to discover ($9.73M), and is the cheapest of the three in 59% of simulated incidents. It assumes the firm can negotiate while restoring; leak deadlines or rising demands can remove that option.
The firm’s walk-away point is the largest demand worth paying on day one, before any restore has been tried; the decision maps on this site describe that day-one choice. At the most likely values it is $2.39M, just below the $2.5M demand, so the firm is close to indifferent. Allowing for uncertainty in every input, paying a $2.5M demand on day one is cheaper than restoring in 64% of simulated incidents: with today’s restore times, this firm is often a rational payer. Each day cut from restore time lowers the walk-away point by about $0.31M. About $0.73M of it assumes that paying lowers the chance of a leak; if it does not, the walk-away point falls to $1.66M.

How to read the table. Each row is one input to the cost model. The base column is the single value used for the worked example above. The range column is how uncertain we are: a triangular range gives the lowest, highest and most likely values, and a Beta range describes a probability with its average. The last column says where the value comes from; “Firm assumption” means it is set for this synthetic firm.
What the table tells you. Most inputs are judgments that the firm would replace with its own figures, especially outage cost per day and restore time. Probabilities such as backup credibility and decryptor reliability are uncertain, which is why the site tests the whole range rather than one point. The Governance page lists who would own each assumption and what should trigger a review.







NoteThe walk-away formula





Expected outage if we refuse, where backups work with probability \(b\): \[E[T] = b\,T_r + (1-b)\,T_{fail}\]
Expected cost of refusing: \[C_{refuse} = c\,E[T] + p_{np}K_{leak}\]
Expected cost of paying demand \(D\). The decryptor works with probability \(q\); otherwise we fall back to restoring: \[C_{pay}(D) = D(1+s\kappa) + K_{pay} + c\,[\,d_{pay} + q\,T_d + (1-q)\,E[T]\,] + p_p K_{leak}\]
Pay only if \(C_{pay}(D) \le C_{refuse}\). Solving for \(D\) gives the walk-away point: \[R^* = \frac{c\,[\,q\,(E[T]-T_d) - d_{pay}\,] + (p_{np}-p_p)\,K_{leak} - K_{pay}}{1+s\kappa}\]
The demand \(D\) does not appear in \(R^*\); it only decides which side of the line we fall on. \(R^*\) rises in a straight line with restore time, with slope \(c\,q\,b/(1+s\kappa)\). If \(R^* \le 0\), paying is never worth it.

title: The Game
text:
What the crew knows
The crew doesn’t know our walk-away point, so it sets its demand from what it believes about firms like ours, mainly how long they take to restore. It picks the demand that maximizes its expected take: a higher demand earns more when paid but is refused more often. With the belief used here, its opening demand is $2.53M. We set the crew’s starting belief as a firm assumption at the high end of published figures: the median demand across all victims was $1.32M (Sophos, State of Ransomware 2025), and Coveware’s median payment in Q3 2026 was $400K (Coveware, October 2026).
The demand reflects what the crew believes about our restore time, not what our data is worth. Visible resilience lowers the opening number.

text:
What moves the decision

    mutate(role = c("total", rep("component", 3), rep("other", 3)),

}) |> purrr::list_rbind() |>
  mutate(facet = factor(facet_lab[target], levels = facet_lab),

ggplot(d, aes(share, key, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_pct(share)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8) +
  facet_wrap(~facet, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) sub("___.*", "", x)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(total = "#0166CC", component = "#9CC3EE", other = "#B8B8B8"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous("Share of variation explained", labels = scales::label_percent(),
                     limits = c(0, 0.85), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(y = NULL,

       subtitle = "Components of expected outage time shown in light blue") +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))








Figure 2: Share of the variation in the walk-away point, and in the pay-or-not decision, explained by each input on its own; 200,000 simulated incidents. First-order shares show ranking only; interactions are not shown.






How to read the plot. We simulated 200,000 incidents, drawing every input from its range and the demand from a moderate spread. Each bar shows how much of the spread in the result one input explains on its own. The left panel is the walk-away point; the right is the yes-or-no pay decision. Expected outage time (dark blue) combines the three light-blue inputs beneath it, so those bars overlap it; read the chart as a ranking, not as parts of a whole.
What the plot tells you. Expected outage time explains 69% of the variation in the walk-away point, and restore time alone 43%. In the pay decision, expected outage time explains 39% and the demand 15%. That ranking depends on how widely demands vary: if they vary as much as published payments do, the demand comes first (see the Governance page). Either way, restore time sets the threshold the demand is tested against.

title: The Game
text:
The regulatory clock
Paying adds legal exposure; it never removes disclosure. OFAC can impose civil penalties “based on strict liability”, so a sanctions link that surfaces after payment is still a violation (OFAC, 2021). As an NYDFS-covered entity, the firm must report an extortion payment within 24 hours. Within 30 days it must explain in writing why it was necessary, which alternatives were considered and what sanctions diligence was done (23 NYCRR 500.17(c), ComplianceForge summary; DFS filing instructions). The firm is not listed, but its listed clients run their own clock: if a client judges the incident material to it, that client’s Form 8-K, Item 1.05, is due “within four business days” of the determination, whether or not anyone pays (SEC).

title: When Is a Ransom Worth Paying?
text: All money is in $M and all values are illustrative. The firm is synthetic.

title: When Is a Ransom Worth Paying?
text:
Introduction


“If we’re hit, should we pay, and how do we decide before it happens?”


This site works through that question for a 500-person fintech software firm, the same firm as our Defender–Attacker study. A ransomware crew has encrypted the firm’s production platform and copied its client data. The firm must choose between paying the crew’s demand and restoring from backups. We model that choice as a bargaining game in which the crew does not know how badly we need to pay, and learns from what we do.
The answer, in three sentences:

Every firm has a walk-away point: the largest ransom worth paying, after allowing for a decryptor that may fail, sanctions exposure, the costs of paying, and the leak risk that remains either way.
That point is set by how long it takes to restore; the size of the demand only tests it. Each day cut from restore time lowers it by about $0.31M.
Resilience therefore does two jobs: it lowers the cost of an outage, and it makes a “we don’t pay” policy credible, so crews that learn over repeated incidents attack less often.



Display code
lab_x <- 15
labs_df <- wa$boundaries |>
  filter(abs(T_r - lab_x) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(label = c("Weak backups (0.60)", "Our backups (0.80)", "Strong backups (0.95)")[match(b, c(0.6, 0.8, 0.95))])
decision_map(wa$boundaries, 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = wa$boundaries, aes(T_r, R_star, group = b, linewidth = b == 0.8), color = COL_LINE) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.3, `FALSE` = 0.6), guide = "none") +
  geom_label(data = labs_df, aes(T_r, R_star, label = label), fill = "white", label.size = 0,
             size = 3.7, label.padding = unit(0.15, "lines")) +
  annotate("point", x = 10, y = D_BASE, size = 4, color = "white") +
  annotate("point", x = 10, y = D_BASE, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.4, y = D_BASE + 0.45, label = "Our firm today", hjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 29, y = 0.4, label = "Pay", hjust = 1, fontface = "bold", color = "#7a5a12", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 7.5, label = "Don't pay", hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", color = COL_NOPAY, size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Restore time sets the most we should ever pay",
       subtitle = "Walk-away point by restore time, for three levels of backup credibility")








Figure 1: Decision map for the day-one choice. Below a line, paying on day one is cheaper than restoring; above it, restoring is cheaper. The shading shows our firm’s backups. The three lines are three levels of backup credibility, the probability that backups restore cleanly.






How to read the plot. Restore time runs across the bottom and the crew’s demand runs up the side. Each line is our walk-away point at one level of backup credibility. A demand below the line is worth paying; a demand above it is not. The shaded areas show the pay (amber) and don’t-pay (blue) regions for our own backups. The black dot is our firm today: a 10-day restore and a $2.5M demand.
What the plot tells you. Restore time sets where the line sits; the demand only decides which side of it we fall. At the most likely values our firm sits just above its line, with a walk-away point of $2.39M. Allowing for uncertainty in every input, paying a $2.5M demand on day one is cheaper in 64% of simulated incidents: with today’s restore times, this firm is often a rational payer. Weak backups raise the line to $4.32M at a 10-day restore.

title: When Is a Ransom Worth Paying?
text:
Three findings
Restore time sets the threshold. The walk-away point does not depend on the demand at all: restore time sets it, and the demand only tests it. Across 200,000 simulated incidents, expected outage time (restore time, backup credibility and rebuild time combined) explains 69% of the variation in the walk-away point. When demands vary over a moderate range, it also explains more of the pay decision (39%) than the demand does (15%); if demands vary as widely as published payments, the demand comes first (sensitivity table). Cutting restore from 10 to 5 days lowers the walk-away point from $2.39M to $0.84M.
Paying is a poor first move. The decryptor may fail, decryption itself takes days, the stolen data may leak anyway, a sanctions link can surface after payment, and regulators must be told either way. At the most likely values, paying a $2.5M demand on day one costs $10.83M in expectation, against $10.70M for restoring: within about 1% of each other, so the answer depends on the inputs. Restoring first and paying only if backups fail costs $9.23M, less than either.
A credible refusal means fewer attacks, and credibility requires resilience. Crews learn from what we do, and a crew that expects less attacks less often. Over 10 years at a 15% annual attack rate, never paying costs our firm $13.2M against $15.6M for paying case by case. The test comes at the first incident, when a fragile firm with a 21-day restore would save $4.8M by paying. In the model, the extra attacks that one payment invites cost it more (present value $16.2M against $14.0M), so the policy holds, but only if crews favor firms that have paid before. Without that, paying once is cheaper, and only resilience removes the temptation.

title: When Is a Ransom Worth Paying?
text:
Decide before it happens


Display code
tibble::tribble(
  ~Decision, ~`What to set`, ~`Why it matters`,
  "1. Walk-away rule", "Who can invoke a payment, and the walk-away point they must test the demand against",
    "The walk-away point, not the size of the demand, decides whether paying is rational.",
  "2. Restore-time target", "A target for the platform, for example under 5 days, tested at least yearly",
    paste0("Each restore day is worth about ", fmt_m(wa$slope, 2), " of walk-away point; below about ", fmt_num(wa$T0, 1), " days no demand is worth paying."),
  "3. Pre-cleared steps", "Sanctions screening, law-enforcement contact, and the 24-hour NYDFS payment notice",
    "Payment delay and sanctions risk raise the cost of paying; preparation shortens both. As an NYDFS-covered firm, we must report any payment within 24 hours.",
  "4. Default policy", "An internal default of \"we don't pay\", with the narrow exceptions written down",
    "A known refusal means fewer attacks later, but only a policy the firm can afford to keep is believed."
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_width(Decision ~ px(180)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_body(columns = Decision)) |>
  gt_board()




Table 1: Four decisions the board can make before an incident.









Decision
What to set
Why it matters




1. Walk-away rule
Who can invoke a payment, and the walk-away point they must test the demand against
The walk-away point, not the size of the demand, decides whether paying is rational.


2. Restore-time target
A target for the platform, for example under 5 days, tested at least yearly
Each restore day is worth about $0.31M of walk-away point; below about 2.3 days no demand is worth paying.


3. Pre-cleared steps
Sanctions screening, law-enforcement contact, and the 24-hour NYDFS payment notice

An internal default of "we don't pay", with the narrow exceptions written down

How to read the table. Each row is one decision the board can take now, before any incident. The middle column says what to set, and the last column links it to a finding from this analysis. The four rows follow the order of an incident: who decides, how fast we can recover, what must already be cleared with regulators and law enforcement, and what the firm’s default answer is.
What the table tells you. The most important decision is the restore-time target, because it moves the walk-away point more than anything else and makes the no-pay default believable. The other three turn a decision made under pressure into one made in advance. None of them requires predicting the size of the next demand. Each can be rehearsed in a tabletop exercise, so the board can check that the decisions hold before a real incident tests them.


Related work. This study pairs with a related study of the same firm: the Defender–Attacker study shows how a crew chooses which asset to attack. Outage cost here is set at $0.5M per day for this study alone.

How to read the plot. Restore time runs across the bottom and the crew’s demand runs up the side. The solid line is our walk-away point: the most it would be worth paying at each restore time. In the amber area below it, paying is cheaper; in the blue area above it, restoring is cheaper. title: Decision Map & Reputation
section: What each choice teaches the crew
text:
What each choice teaches the crew
Each incident is also a lesson for the crew. A crew that is paid concludes we value our systems more than it guessed, and asks for more next time. A crew that is refused lowers its estimate, and its next demand falls. We simulate a 10-year horizon in which the crew learns from every incident and favors targets that have paid before. For a firm that never pays, lower demands are not the benefit; the benefit is that a crew expecting less attacks less often.
We compare two policies. Pay when worth it means paying whenever, in that incident, the demand is below our walk-away point. Never pay means refusing every time, committed in advance.


Display code
base_grid <- at_p0(p0b)
dp <- bind_rows(
  tibble(series = "Never pay (any firm)", attack = 1:4, demand = rep$demand_seqs$R, policy = "never"),
  base_grid |> filter(policy == "rational", firm != "resilient") |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(demand_1:demand_4, names_to = "attack", values_to = "demand") |>
    transmute(series = paste0(c(typical = "Our firm", fragile = "Fragile firm")[firm], ", pays when worth it"),
              attack = readr::parse_number(attack), demand, policy)
)
ends <- dp |> filter(attack == 4)
ggplot(dp, aes(attack, demand, color = policy, group = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = series), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, color = "white") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = series), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.08, size = 3.9, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = POLICY_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "22"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous("Attack number", breaks = 1:4, limits = c(1, 5.6)) +
  scale_y_continuous("Crew's demand", labels = \(x) paste0("$", x, "M"), limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Refusing pulls the next demand down; paying pushes it up",
       subtitle = "Average demand at each successive attack ($M)")








Figure 2: Average demand the crew posts at each successive attack, by firm and policy, at a 15% annual attack rate.






How to read the plot. Each line follows the crew’s demand from the first attack to the fourth. The blue line is a firm that never pays; because the crew learns only from refusals, its path is the same for any firm. The orange lines are firms that pay when the demand is below their walk-away point: dashed for our firm, solid for the fragile one. Points are averages over the simulated paths that reach each attack.
What the plot tells you. Refusal teaches the crew that we are a poor prospect: its demand falls from $2.53M to $0.87M by the third attack. The fragile firm, which pays almost every time, sees demands climb to $4.59M by the fourth. In one survey, 78% of payers were attacked again and 63% of those were asked for more, though it does not compare payers with non-payers (Infosecurity Magazine, February 2024).

gap = f => now.find(d => d.firm === f && d.policy === "rational").cost_10y - now.find(d => d.firm === f && d.policy === "never").cost_10y

html`<div class="slider-sentence">At a <b>${rate}%</b> annual attack rate, a credible no-pay policy ${word(gap("typical"))} our firm about <b>$${Math.abs(gap("typical")).toFixed(1)}M</b> over 10 years and ${word(gap("fragile"))} the fragile firm about <b>$${Math.abs(gap("fragile")).toFixed(1)}M</b>.</div>`



































How to read the plot. Each row is a firm profile: resilient (4-day restore, 0.90 backup credibility), our firm (10 days, 0.80) and fragile (21 days, 0.60). Blue dots are never pay; orange dots pay when worth it. The resilient firm never pays under either policy, so it has one gray dot. Each label gives the expected 10-year cost and expected number of attacks. Drag the slider to change the annual chance of an attack.
What the plot tells you. At 15%, never paying saves our firm about $2.4M and the fragile firm about $5.9M over 10 years. The saving comes from fewer attacks: 2.2 in 10 years for the fragile firm if it pays when worth it, against 1.2 if it never pays. The saving grows quickly with the attack rate. The resilient firm would refuse every demand anyway, so for it the policy costs nothing to keep.

The more often you expect to be attacked, the more a reputation for refusing is worth. At a 5% annual rate, the fragile firm is slightly better off paying case by case (by $1.2M over 10 years), because it is rarely attacked often enough for reputation to matter. From about 9% upward, never paying is cheaper for both firms.

title: Decision Map & Reputation
section: Why the policy must be credible
text:
Why the policy must be credible
A no-pay policy is only worth what the crew believes about it, and a policy breaks under pressure when breaking it pays. In the moment, a fragile firm facing the first $2.53M demand saves about $4.8M by paying, because its walk-away point is $6.87M.
To test whether that temptation should win, we compare never paying with paying once, at the first incident, and never again. Costs are in present value at a 8% discount rate, so the saving on the day counts in full and later attacks count for less. For the fragile firm, paying once costs $16.2M over 10 years against $14.0M for never paying: the extra attacks it invites outweigh the saving, so the policy is credible, by a margin of $2.2M. For our firm the margin is $1.3M. If crews ignore past payments, the result reverses: paying once saves the fragile firm $3.2M, and the policy is not credible.
A resilient firm faces no such test. Its walk-away point is −$0.67M, so refusing is also its cheapest move on the day. Its policy is believed because it never has to be enforced against its own interest. Resilience is what turns a stated policy into a believed one.

title: Reproducibility
text: Every number on this site comes from synthetic inputs in params.yaml and data/, and from results computed by the scripts in R/. Nothing is downloaded, and every random draw is seeded, so running the same commit with the same package versions gives the same results. The pages never compute the heavy results themselves: they read cached results from data/results/. The decision-map slider recomputes the closed-form walk-away point in the browser, using a JavaScript file that the pipeline checks against R. This page explains how to rebuild the results, lists the inputs with their checksums, shows the tests, and records the software environment.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Quick start

Clone the GitHub repository and open the project folder in RStudio or Positron.
Restore the packages with renv::restore() (see Software environment). You need R 4.3 or later and Quarto 1.5 or later.
From a terminal in the project root, rebuild the results, run the tests and render the site:

Rscript R/run_all.R
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
quarto render
The rendered site is written to docs/. Run R/run_all.R with Rscript from a terminal, not with source() in an R console: it ends with quit(), which would close your session. It exits with an error status if any diagnostic fails. To look at the site locally, run quarto preview, which renders it and opens it in your browser. The sliders need a web server, so they don’t work when a page is opened straight from disk; on GitHub Pages they work as is.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Caching

Results cache (data/results/*.rds). Written by R/run_all.R and read by every page. It is not invalidated automatically: after changing params.yaml or any script, rerun Rscript R/run_all.R. The files are committed to git so the site renders from a fresh clone.
Quarto freeze (_freeze/). _quarto.yml sets freeze: auto, so a full quarto render re-executes a page only when that page’s .qmd file changes. Edits to R/ scripts or new results do not count as a change. After rerunning the pipeline, render each page explicitly (for example quarto render governance.qmd) or delete _freeze/ first. _freeze/ is not committed.
